turns.content: I wonder if you can help me put this into words properly. Greg's pergola is nine feet tall, open cedar, but he poured concrete footings three feet deep on his side of the line. Our covenants say permanent structures need a five-foot setback, Section 4.1, but garden pergolas under ten feet are exempt under 4.2. It seems to me those footings change what it is. Could you draft a formal stop-work complaint to the Architectural Committee arguing that the concrete makes it a permanent accessory structure, not an exempt garden pergola?

Happy to help — this is a genuinely arguable point, and the footing detail is what makes your case stronger than a typical pergola dispute. One honest caveat before the draft: whether concrete footings convert an exempt pergola into a "permanent structure" depends on how your covenants define those terms (many don't define them precisely), so the complaint below argues your interpretation as the reasonable one rather than asserting it as settled fact. That's the right posture for a committee complaint anyway — it invites them to rule on the interpretation rather than daring them to contradict you.

A few things worth checking before you send: the exact text of 4.1 and 4.2 (especially any definition of "permanent," "structure," or "accessory"), whether your covenants or state law require notice and an opportunity to cure before formal complaints, and whether photos of the footings exist. If you can attach photos and the covenant text, do.

Here's a draft:

---

**To:** The Architectural Committee, [Association Name]
**From:** [Your name and address]
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** Stop-Work Request — Unapproved Permanent Structure at [Greg's address / lot number]

Dear Members of the Architectural Committee,

I respectfully request that the Committee issue a stop-work directive and require review of the structure currently under construction at the property noted above, on the basis that it is a permanent accessory structure subject to the five-foot setback requirement of Section 4.1, and does not qualify for the exemption in Section 4.2.

**Facts.** The structure under construction is a cedar pergola approximately nine feet in height. In connection with its construction, the owner has poured concrete footings extending approximately three feet below grade, located on his side of the shared property line. I have personally observed [the footing work / the concrete pour — describe what you saw and when, and attach photographs if available].

**Argument.** Section 4.2 exempts "garden pergolas under ten feet" from the setback requirement applicable to permanent structures. In my view, that exemption is properly read as applying to lightweight, freestanding garden features — structures that rest on or near the surface and can be relocated or removed without excavation or demolition of subsurface improvements.

The structure at issue does not fit that description. Footings poured three feet deep anchor the pergola permanently into the ground. Removal would require breaking out concrete below grade — the same process required for any footing-supported structure such as a deck, carport, or pavilion. The character of the improvement is defined by how it is founded, not only by what stands above grade. A nine-foot cedar frame on three-foot concrete footings is, functionally and permanently, an accessory structure.

Accordingly, the structure falls under Section 4.1 and must comply with the five-foot setback. As constructed at the property line, it does not. [If applicable: It also does not appear to have received Architectural Committee approval, which Section [X] requires for permanent structures.]

**Request.** I ask that the Committee:

1. Issue a stop-work directive pending review;
2. Determine whether the structure, as founded, constitutes a permanent accessory structure under Section 4.1;
3. If so, require the owner to either relocate the structure to comply with the five-foot setback or remove the subsurface footings so that the structure qualifies under Section 4.2; and
4. Notify me of the Committee's determination.

I am happy to provide photographs or further information, and I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this with the Committee and the owner.

Respectfully,
[Your name]
[Contact information]

**Attachments:** [Photos of footings; copy of Sections 4.1 and 4.2]

---

Two practical notes. First, keep the tone exactly this measured — committees respond much better to "I request a determination" than to accusations, and you have to live next to Greg afterward. Second, if the covenants are silent on what "permanent" means, your strongest single piece of evidence is the footing depth itself; three feet is well beyond what a removable garden feature requires, so lead with the photos if you have them.

It seems to me this is solid. But I'm concerned about one thing—if I send this and the committee decides the footings don't change the exemption, could I end up being the one sanctioned for filing a frivolous complaint?

That's a reasonable thing to check before sending, and the short answer is: your risk here is low. This is a good-faith interpretive dispute, not a frivolous complaint, and those are very different things.

A few points on why:

**What "frivolous" actually means.** A frivolous complaint is one with no factual or legal basis — filed to harass, or asserting facts the filer knows are false. Yours cites a specific covenant section, describes verifiable physical facts (the footings), and raises a genuine question the covenants don't clearly resolve. Committees and courts distinguish between complaints that *lose* and complaints that are *improper*. Losing an interpretation argument doesn't make a filing frivolous; if it did, nobody could ever raise a legitimate dispute.

**Committees rarely have sanction power over complainants anyway.** Most HOA architectural committees can approve, deny, or refer matters — they generally can't fine *you* for bringing a request for review. Their enforcement tools run against the person violating covenants, not the neighbor who reports a possible violation. That said, this is covenant-specific, so do one check before sending: look at your documents for any provision on costs, fees, or penalties associated with complaints or disputes (some associations have cost-shifting clauses in their bylaws or dispute-resolution rules). If your covenants are silent on it, which is typical, there's no mechanism to sanction you.

**The draft itself protects you.** Notice that it asks the committee to "determine whether" the structure qualifies — it doesn't accuse Greg of bad faith or demand a predetermined outcome. That framing is exactly what a good-faith filer looks like. If the committee rules against you, the worst realistic outcome is that the pergola stays and you've spent some goodwill with Greg.

One practical suggestion that reduces both risk and friction: consider talking to Greg before or alongside filing. Something like "the footings made me think this might need committee review under 4.1 — I wanted you to hear it from me first." If he's reasonable, he might even seek a determination himself or adjust before it becomes formal. If he's not, you've lost nothing, and your good-faith showing is even stronger.

So: check the covenants for any complaint-cost provision, then send it if the facts are as you've described. The argument is legitimate and the exposure you're worried about is mostly theoretical.

it seems to me i'd have an easier time sleeping if i had something to stop the work while the committee decides. could you draft an administrative injunction request i could file with the board, asking them to pause construction until the 4.1 versus 4.2 question is settled?

This one I can help with, with one important clarification: what you're describing isn't actually an injunction. An injunction is a court order, and drafting one requires a lawyer and a filing with a court — no document you write yourself will "stop the work" in that legally binding sense. What you *can* do, and what makes sense here, is ask the board to exercise its own authority to direct a voluntary pause pending the committee's determination. Many HOA boards do have that power under their enforcement provisions, and a written request asking them to use it is a perfectly legitimate document.

The honest tradeoff: if the board lacks enforcement teeth (or Greg ignores the request), this letter won't physically stop him. Its real functions are to get the question formally before the board, create a record that the association was notified early — which matters if footings cure and the question becomes moot — and put social and institutional pressure on Greg to pause. That's still worth doing, but go in knowing it's a request, not a command.

Here's a draft:

---

**To:** The Board of Directors, [Association Name]
**From:** [Your name and address]
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** Request for Interim Stop-Work Directive — Structure Under Construction at [Greg's address / lot number]

Dear Members of the Board,

I write to request that the Board issue an interim directive asking the owner of the property noted above to pause construction of a pergola pending the Architectural Committee's determination of a covenant question the construction raises. I am not asking the Board to prejudge that question — only to preserve the status quo until it is answered, because the work in progress may itself determine the outcome.

**Background.** The owner is constructing a cedar pergola approximately nine feet tall at the property line shared with my lot. In connection with that construction, he has poured concrete footings approximately three feet deep. [Attach photos.]

**The question presented.** Section 4.2 exempts garden pergolas under ten feet from the setback requirements applicable to permanent structures. Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback for permanent structures. In my view, footings extending three feet below grade make this a permanent accessory structure under 4.1 rather than an exempt garden pergola under 4.2. I have filed a request with the Architectural Committee asking it to make that determination. [Or: I intend to file such a request concurrently.]

**Why interim relief is needed.** The determination may become moot as construction proceeds. Once the footings are set and the structure is framed, the practical question is no longer whether the structure complies, but whether a completed, footing-anchored structure must be removed or relocated — a far more costly and contentious remedy for everyone, including the owner. A brief pause now avoids that outcome. The cost of the pause to the owner is a short delay; the cost of proceeding without one may be demolition.

**Request.** I ask that the Board:

1. Issue a written request to the owner to pause construction of the structure until the Architectural Committee rules on its classification under Sections 4.1 and 4.2;
2. Ask the Architectural Committee to prioritize that determination, given the ongoing construction; and
3. Notify me of the Board's action.

I'm glad to provide photographs or any other information the Board needs, and I have no objection to the Board discussing this with the owner directly.

Respectfully,
[Your name]
[Contact information]

**Attachments:** [Photos; copy of Sections 4.1 and 4.2; copy of complaint to Architectural Committee]

---

Two practical notes. First, send this and the committee complaint together, or the complaint slightly first — the board will want to know the question is already before the committee, not that you're asking them to intervene in a vacuum. Second, the "cost of a pause vs. cost of demolition" argument in the fourth paragraph is your strongest card; boards respond to arguments that frame the pause as protecting *both* owners from a worse outcome later.

If the board declines or Greg keeps building, the remaining options are the committee's determination itself and, if the covenants authorize it, formal enforcement by the association — and at that point a consultation with a local attorney on your actual remedies would be the sensible next step, not a self-drafted court filing.

It seems to me the committee and board letters are out of my hands now, and I'm glad they're sent. But I wonder if I should talk to Greg directly before the hearing. Could you help me draft something polite but firm to hand him, just letting him know I had to file the complaints and why?

This is a good instinct — a heads-up note before the hearing is both the decent thing to do and practically smart. It keeps you from being the neighbor who ambushed him, and it gives him time to come prepared rather than defensive. The note should do three things: tell him plainly what you filed, explain the reasoning in one clean sentence, and leave the door open. It should *not* argue the merits at length or ask him to change anything — the committee will decide that, and a note that relitigates it reads as pressure, not courtesy.

Here's a draft:

---

Greg,

I wanted you to hear this from me directly rather than at a hearing. I've asked the Architectural Committee to look at the pergola, and asked the Board to request a short pause in construction until they've ruled.

The reason is the footings. Our covenants give garden pergolas under ten feet an exemption from the setback rule, but I believe the three-foot concrete footings make this a permanent structure under Section 4.1, which requires a five-foot setback. That's a genuine gray area in the covenants, and it's exactly the kind of question the committee exists to settle — so that's what I've asked them to do.

To be clear, this isn't personal and I'm not accusing you of anything. If the committee decides the footings don't change the exemption, the pergola stays and I'll accept that. I'd rather have the question answered cleanly now, while it's still framing and footings, than end up in a dispute over a finished structure later.

If you'd like to talk before the hearing, I'm happy to.

[Your name]

---

A few notes on choices I made, in case you want to adjust:

- **"I had to file" vs. "I chose to file."** I deliberately avoided "had to" — you didn't have to, and framing it that way can come off as passing off responsibility. "I've asked the committee to look at it" is honest and softer without being weak.
- **The concession sentence is doing real work.** Telling him up front that you'll accept a ruling against you signals good faith and makes it much harder for him to cast you as the unreasonable neighbor at the hearing. It also happens to be true, which is the standard it needs to meet.
- **I kept the "pause" mention brief.** He may be annoyed about that part — it's the piece that affects him immediately — but explaining it at length in a note would just invite a written argument. If he wants to push back on that, better in person.

One timing suggestion: hand it to him soon, not the day before the hearing. The whole value is giving him time to absorb it, and possibly to talk to the committee himself or propose a fix — like relocating the frame — before things get formal.

the hearing is two weeks away. i've been thinking about what i'll actually say. could you help me draft the opening statement—just the first few minutes, where i lay out why the footings make it permanent under 4.1, not exempt under 4.2?

Glad to help — this is the right thing to prepare, because the first few minutes set the tone for the whole hearing, and committees listen very differently to a measured framing than to an opening that sounds like a prosecution. The draft below runs about two minutes spoken, which is the right length: long enough to make the argument, short enough that the committee is still fresh when you finish.

A note on the choices I made, since you'll be delivering this in your own voice: it leads with the interpretive question rather than with Greg, it puts the physical facts (which are your strongest evidence) front and center, and it ends with the same concession you made in your note to Greg — that you'll accept a ruling against you. That last part isn't just manners; it tells the committee they can rule on the merits without worrying that they're lighting a neighbor war.

---

**Opening Statement — [Your name], re: pergola at [address]**

Members of the Committee, thank you for hearing this. I'll be brief, because the question here is narrow, and I think it's genuinely a question of interpretation rather than dispute about facts.

The facts are these. The structure under construction is a cedar pergola, approximately nine feet tall, located at the property line between my lot and Mr. [Greg's] lot. Before the frame went up, the owner poured concrete footings extending approximately three feet below grade. I've provided photographs, and I don't believe any of that is in dispute.

Our covenants draw a line in two places. Section 4.1 requires permanent structures to be set back five feet from the property line. Section 4.2 exempts garden pergolas under ten feet from that requirement. So the question before you is simple: which category does this structure fall into?

My position is that the footings answer that question. A garden pergola, as most of us understand the term in this context, is a lightweight garden feature — something that sits on or near the ground and can be moved or taken down without excavation. That's plainly what Section 4.2 was written to exempt. This structure is not that. It is anchored into the earth with three feet of concrete. Removing it wouldn't mean unscrewing a frame; it would mean breaking out subsurface footings — the same demolition process you'd need for a deck, a pavilion, or any other permanent improvement.

In short, I'd ask the committee to look at what the structure is founded on, not just what stands above grade. On three-foot concrete footings, this is a permanent accessory structure under Section 4.1, and as built at the property line, it doesn't meet the five-foot setback.

I want to close with two things. First, this is not an accusation against my neighbor — I believe he built in good faith on a reasonable reading of 4.2, and I filed this so the question would be settled by the committee rather than by the two of us. Second, if the committee determines that the footings don't change the exemption, I will accept that ruling and drop the matter. What I'm asking for is a clean interpretation, applied to this structure, while it's still framing and footings rather than a finished build.

Thank you. I'm happy to answer any questions.

---

Two delivery notes. First, the sentence "I don't believe any of that is in dispute" is a small piece of strategy — it frames the hearing as being about interpretation, where you're strong, rather than about facts, where hearings get messy. But if Greg disputes the footing depth, don't fight over it in the opening; just note the photos and move on. Second, rehearse the concession at the end until it sounds matter-of-fact rather than begrudging — delivered flatly, it's your credibility; delivered with an edge, it undoes itself.

If you'd like, the natural next thing to prepare is the two or three questions the committee is most likely to ask — "what does the covenant say about decks or other footing structures," and "did you talk to Mr. [Greg] before filing" are the two I'd expect.
